overview.body:
**Ymir** ​(*ymir*) — ‌Primordial Giant, ‌Chaos · ​Twin, screamer ​(from *ymijaz) ​— belongs ​to the ​Norse tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Primordial ​Giant, Chaos". ‌The name ​means ‌"Twin, screamer ​(from *ymijaz)"[^1].

​Ymir is ​the first ​living thing ​in the ‌Norse cosmos ​— the ‌frost-giant who ​condensed out ‌of the ​dripping rime ‌where the ​heat ‌of Múspell ​met the ​ice of ‌Niflheimr in ‌the yawning ‌void of ​Ginnungagap. He ​is the ‌ancestor of ​every jotunn, ​the cow ‌Auðhumla's nursling, ​and finally ​the raw ‌material ​of creation ‌itself: Óðinn, ​Vili, and ​Vé kill ​him, and ​from his ‌body build ‌the world ​— flesh ‌to earth, ​blood to ​sea, bones ‌to mountains, ‌skull to ‌sky.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as **Ymir** ​and serves ​its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/ymir/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form *ymir* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 5–8 (Ginnungagap, Élivágar, Auðhumla and Búri, the killing and the making of the world); Skáldskaparmál (kennings and the þulur naming Aurgelmir, Brimir, Bláinn).
Rigveda 10.90, the Puruṣasūkta (the world from the dismembered primeval man) — the Sanskrit structural parallel.

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Younger ​Futhark ​as ​**ᚢᛘᛁᚱ**. Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"Twin, ​screamer ‌(from *ymijaz)"[^1].

​The ‌reconstructed ​proto-form ‌is ​*ymijaz* (proto-indo-european, ​"Twin, ​screamer"). ​Twin, ​screamer ‌(from *ymijaz)

​The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*ymir* ​survives only ‌because ​the ‌early ​domain-name ​system could ‌not ‌carry ‌diacritics; ​it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, ​not ‌an ​ancient spelling. ​The ‌Unicode ​restoration ‌**Ymir** recovers ​the ​full ​diacritic ​detail ‌of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ​in ​the address ‌bar. ‌The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description ​computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**y** ​→ ‌**Y** ​— ‌Same
- **m** ​→ ‌**m** ​— ‌Same
- ‌**i** → ​**i** ​— ​Same
- ​**r** ‌→ **r** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈy.mir/** ‌— Old ​Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- **Y** ​— Close front ​rounded vowel [y], ​the sound of ‌German ü ​or French u ​— lips rounded ‌as for 'oo' ​while the tongue ‌says 'ee'
- **-m-** ​— Voiced ‌bilabial nasal [m], ​single and short, ​as in English ​'mound'
- **-i** — ​Short close front ​[i], unrounded, ‌the vowel of ​English 'bit'
- **-r** ‌— Trilled alveolar ​[r] of the ‌nominative ending, ​sounded fully as ‌in modern Icelandic

​For the modern ‌speaker, the closest ​approximation is: 'EE-meer' ​with rounded ‌lips — say ‌'ee' while pursing ‌the mouth as ​for 'oo' (the ​Old Norse y ‌is German ​ü), then a ​short 'i' and ‌a fully trilled ​final r.

Kindred ​and historical forms ‌of the ​name:

- **Old Norse** ‌— Ymir, the ​primordial giant; the ​þulur also know ​him as Aurgelmir, ​'mud-bellow', Brimir, ‌and Bláinn.
- **Old ‌Norse (verb)** — ​ymja, 'to scream, ‌roar, resound' — ​the verbal root ​behind the ‌strongest etymology of ‌the name.
- **Sanskrit** ‌— Yama, the ‌first mortal and ​king of the ‌dead, whose ​name means 'twin' ​— the comparandum ​of the alternative, ‌debated 'twin' etymology.
- ​**Modern Icelandic** ​— Ymir, the ​name's unbroken living ‌form.

Ymir is ​a plain restoration ​by the mechanical ​rule: the ‌normalized Old Norse ​form is already ‌plain ASCII — ​there is no ‌diacritic and no ​distinctive letter ‌for the ASCII ‌alphabet to lose. ​The giant's cosmic ​scale vastly outruns ​his name's orthography; ​only the ‌capital distinguishes the ‌restored form from ​the input.

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger Futhark ​as **ᚢᛘᛁᚱ**.[^1]

​The scholarly ​transliteration ​is *umir*.

​The rendering ‌proceeds step ​by step:

- ​ᚢ (úr) ‌writes ​the rounded ‌back vowels ​/u, o, ‌ø, ǫ, ​y/ and ​/w/
- ​ᛘ (maðr) ​writes /m/
- ​ᛁ (ís) ‌writes both ​/i/ ‌and /e/
- ​The spelling ‌umir is ​a normalized ‌phonetic reconstruction; ​Younger ‌Futhark does ​not distinguish ​voiced/voiceless stops ‌or separate ‌short and ‌long ​vowels

The ​normalized Old ‌Norse form ​is **Ymir** ​— already ‌plain ​ASCII, with ​no diacritic ‌or distinctive ​letter for ‌the restoration ​to ​recover; in ​the Younger ​Futhark the ‌name would ‌have been ​carved ‌ᚢᛘᛁᛦ (úr ​ᚢ writing ​y as ‌it writes ‌u, then ‌m, ‌i, and ​ᛦ the ‌final nominative ​-r). Because ​the name ​is ‌pure ASCII, ​its domain ​was registered ​long ago ‌in ​the ordinary ​way: **ymir.com ​is held ‌by a ​third party ‌outside ​the PuniCodex ‌collection and ​is watched ‌for release** ‌— no ​form ​of the ​name is ​currently owned, ‌and this ‌temple claims ​none.

Poetic Edda (Eddukvæði), ed. Neckel-Kuhn; trans. Carolyn Larrington, Oxford World's Classics (2014), 1270.
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.
A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic, Oxford, 1910.

domains.body:
Ymir is ​the first ‌living thing ‌in the ​Norse cosmos ​— the ​frost-giant who ​condensed out of ​the dripping ‌rime where ​the heat ​of Múspell ‌met the ​ice of ‌Niflheimr in ​the yawning void ‌of Ginnungagap. ​He is ​the ancestor ​of every ​jotunn, the ​cow Auðhumla's ‌nursling, and finally ​the raw ‌material of ​creation itself: ‌Óðinn, Vili, ​and Vé ‌kill him, ​and from his ‌body build ​the world ​— flesh ‌to earth, ‌blood to ‌sea, bones ​to mountains, ​skull to sky.[^1]

### ‌Ginnungagap

The ​yawning void ​before creation ‌— the ​charged emptiness ​between the ‌ice-world of Niflheimr ​and the ‌fire-world of ​Múspell where ​Ymir first ​took shape.

### ​Auðhumla

The ‌primeval cow whose ‌four rivers ​of milk ‌fed Ymir, ​and who ​licked the ‌salty rime-stones ‌until Búri, ‌grandfather of the ‌gods, emerged ​from the ‌ice.

### The ​Dismemberment

Slain ​by Óðinn, ​Vili, and ‌Vé, Ymir becomes ​the world: ​flesh earth, ​blood sea, ‌bones mountains, ​hair trees, ​skull sky, ​brains the clouds.

### ‌Bergelmir's Flood

​So much ‌blood poured ​from Ymir's ‌wound that ​the whole ‌race of ‌frost-giants drowned — ​all but ​Bergelmir and ​his wife, ​who rode ‌out the ‌deluge on ​their lúðr.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 5–8 (Ginnungagap, Élivágar, Auðhumla and Búri, the killing and the making of the world); Skáldskaparmál (kennings and the þulur naming Aurgelmir, Brimir, Bláinn).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Ymir concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ​recurring attributes, ‌each ​a compressed ​statement ‌about the ​name:[^1]

- ‌**Ginnungagap** ​— The ‌yawning ​void at ​the ​world's beginning ​— ​the unmade ‌space ​where ‌fire and ​ice ‌first traded ​breath
- ‌**Auðhumla** — ​The ‌cow who ​feeds ​the ‌giant and ‌frees ‌the gods ​— ​plenty and ‌creation ​flowing from ​the ‌same ​rime
- **The ​dismembered ‌body** — ​The ‌map of ​the ​world ​written in ​one ‌corpse: every ‌landscape ​a part ‌of ​Ymir, the ​cosmos ‌as ‌anatomy
- **The ‌blood-flood** ‌— The ​deluge ‌from Ymir's ​wound ​that drowns ​the ‌frost-giants ​— destruction ​and ​sea-making in ‌a ​single act
- ​**The ​four sky-dwarfs** ‌— ​Norðri, ‌Suðri, Austri, ​and ‌Vestri, set ​by ‌the gods ‌to ​hold Ymir's ​skull ​up ​at the ‌four ‌corners of ​heaven

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

mythology.body:
Ymir has no adventures and ​no cult: his mythology is cosmogony entire. He exists to ‌be first — first life, first giant, first death ‌— and the corpus treats him less as a character ​than as a fact of physics: the being out of ​whom everything had to be made, because before him ​there was nothing to make it from.[^1]

### Out of the ​Rime (Gylfaginning 5–6 · Vafþrúðnismál 20–21)

Before the world ​there was Ginnungagap, the yawning void, with the frozen rivers ‌of Niflheimr to the north and the sparks of Múspell ​to the south. Where the heat met the rime, ​Snorri says, the hoar-frost melted and dripped, and the drops ‌quickened into the shape of a man: Ymir, whom ​the frost-giants call Aurgelmir. Vafþrúðnismál gives the older verse version ‌— from Élivágar's waves shot poison-drops that froze and grew, ​until a jotunn arose from them.

He was no ‌god and no friend to gods: Snorri calls him and ​all his line evil. Yet everything that follows in ​the cosmos presupposes him — the first living being is ​the first material, and creation in the Norse telling is ​not ex nihilo but a reworking of what already ​is.[^2]

### The Self-Begetting Giant (Vafþrúðnismál 29, 32–33)

The scene is ‌the wisdom contest of Vafþrúðnismál: Óðinn, disguised as Gagnráðr, ​stakes his head on questions the giant Vafþrúðnir cannot answer, ‌and one of them is this — how did ​Ymir beget children when he knew no giantess? The giant ‌answers with the strangest genealogy in the corpus: from under ​the primeval giant's arm grew a man and a ‌woman together, and one of his legs begot a six-headed ​son on the other. The jotnar multiply from the ‌giant's own body — parthenogenesis in sweat and limb, male ​and female folded into one hermaphroditic mass. Snorri repeats the ​detail in Gylfaginning 6, and the two versions agree ‌on the essentials.

This is why Ymir is the ancestor ‌of all giants: not through a wife but through ‌himself. Hyndluljóð states the doctrine flatly — all the giants ​descend from Ymir. The jotnar are not a rival tribe ​to the gods; they are the older generation of ‌the same world-substance, and the self-begetting giant who needs no ​partner is the myth's image of a cosmos that ​has not yet learned to divide.

### Auðhumla and Búri (Gylfaginning ‌6)

Ymir did not starve. From the same dripping rime ​came the cow Auðhumla, and four rivers of milk ​ran from her udder to feed him. She herself licked ‌the salty rime-stones, and as she licked, a man's ​shape emerged from the ice — hair the first day, ‌head the second, the whole man the third: Búri, ​strong and fair, who begot Borr, and Borr married Bestla ​the giant's daughter, and their sons were Óðinn, Vili, and ​Vé.

The detail is the myth's quiet hinge: gods ​and giants rise from the same frost within days of ‌one another, and the gods' grandmother is herself a ‌giantess. Snorri's genealogy makes the coming killing not a war ​on strangers but the oldest kind of violence — the ‌young order turning on the body of the old.

### ​The Making of the World (Grímnismál 40–41 · Gylfaginning 8)

​Óðinn, Vili, and Vé kill Ymir, and from his ‌body they make the world. Grímnismál gives the catalogue in ‌verse: from Ymir's flesh the earth was shaped, from his ‌blood the sea, from his bones the mountains, from ‌his hair the trees, and from his skull the sky; ​from his eyelashes the gods made Miðgarðr as a ‌defence against the giants, and from his brains the heavy, ​wind-driven clouds. Snorri adds the maggots in the flesh, made ​rational by the gods' decree as the dwarfs, and ​the four dwarfs — Norðri, Suðri, Austri, Vestri — set ‌to hold up the skull-vault of heaven at its ​corners.

So much blood ran from the wound that it ​became a deluge, and the whole race of frost-giants ​drowned in it — all but one. Bergelmir, Ymir's heir ‌in the verse line, rode out the flood with his ​wife on his lúðr, and from them the jotnar ​were born again. Creation's first act is a killing, and ​its first catastrophe follows immediately: the world is made, ‌and nearly unmade of giants, in a single stroke.

### 'In ​Early Days, When Ymir Dwelled' (Völuspá 3–5)

The völva of ‌Völuspá opens her memory with him: 'It was in ​early days, when Ymir dwelled; there was no sand nor ‌sea nor cool waves, no earth existed, nor heaven ​above, a yawning void there was, and grass nowhere.' The ‌giant is the poem's first named being — the datum ‌from which the seeress's whole vision of time unfolds.

​Then Burr's sons lift up the earth, and the ordering ​begins. Völuspá never stages the killing; it simply places ​Ymir on the far side of a before and an ​after. That placement is his function everywhere in the corpus: ‌he is the name Norse tradition gives to the ‌raw, unworked world — and the proof that even the ​raw world had a body.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 5–8 (Ginnungagap, Élivágar, Auðhumla and Búri, the killing and the making of the world); Skáldskaparmál (kennings and the þulur naming Aurgelmir, Brimir, Bláinn).
Rigveda 10.90, the Puruṣasūkta (the world from the dismembered primeval man) — the Sanskrit structural parallel.

syncretism.body:
Ymir stands ​at the ‌centre of the ‌best-known comparative debate ​in Germanic ​mythology: the Indo-European ​dismemberment cosmogony. The ​Sanskrit parallel ​is exact in ‌structure — ​Rigveda 10.90, the ​Puruṣasūkta, makes the ‌world from ​the sacrifice of ‌the primeval man ​Puruṣa, whose ‌breath became wind, ​head sky, ​feet earth — ​and scholars from ​the nineteenth ​century onward have ‌read Ymir as ​the Norse ‌reflex of the ​same inherited ‌pattern, most fully ​in Bruce Lincoln's ‌studies of ​Indo-European creation myth. ‌The name itself ​is contested: ​the strong philological ‌line derives ‌Ymir from the ‌Old Norse verb ​ymja, 'to ​scream, roar, resound' ‌— the Roarer ​— while ​the alternative connects ‌it to ​Indo-European *yemo-, 'twin' ​(Sanskrit Yama, Latin ‌geminus), which ​would make the ‌hermaphroditic, self-begetting giant ​the 'Twin'. ​Simek, de Vries, ​and Lindow ​all register the ‌dispute without settling ‌it; this ​temple records both. ‌Tacitus supplies the ​Germanic corroboration ​— Germania chapter ‌2 has ‌the peoples of ‌Germania sing of ‌Tuisto, 'a ​god born of ‌the earth', whose ​name is ​regularly read as ​'twin, two-fold' ‌— as the ​ancestor of Mannus ​and all ​the tribes.[^1]

Kindred ‌figures in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include [[audhumla|Auðhumla]] ​(primeval nourisher ‌and frost giant), ​[[angrboda|Angrboða]] (chaos / ‌primordial / ​world serpent), [[apep|ꜥꜣpp]] ‌(chaos / primordial ​/ world ‌serpent), [[chaos|Cháos]] (chaos ‌/ primordial ​/ world serpent), ​[[hati|Hati]] (chaos / ​primordial / ​world serpent), and ‌[[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]] (chaos / ‌primordial / ​world serpent).

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

cultural-legacy.body: Ymir's ​afterlife runs ‌wherever ‌Norse myth ​is ​retold at ​scale. ​Richard Wagner's ​ring ‌cycle built ​its ​world-music on ‌the ​same dismembered-primordial ‌logic, ​and the ‌giant ​survives under ​his ​own name ​across ​modern popular ‌culture: ​Robert E. ‌Howard's ​'The Frost-Giant's ‌Daughter' ​(1934) makes ‌its ​heroine the ‌daughter ​of Ymir, ​Marvel ‌Comics has ‌kept ‌Ymir the ​frost ​giant in ‌print ​since 1962 ​as ‌an antagonist ​of ​Thor, and ‌the ​name recurs ‌across ​fantasy games ​from ​Dungeons & ​Dragons ‌onward wherever ‌frost-giants ​are wanted. ‌In ​scholarship the ​figure ‌anchors the ‌comparative ‌project — ‌Lincoln's ​Myth, Cosmos, ‌and ​Society built ​its ​account of ‌Indo-European ​creation ideology ​around ​the Ymir ‌material. ​Modern Heathenry ​reads ​him as ‌the ​necessary first ‌matter ​of the ‌cosmos: ​not a ‌villain ‌to be ​erased ​but the ​body ​the world ‌is ‌still made ​of.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

archaeology.body: Ymir ​is an ‌entirely textual ‌being: ​no runestone ​invokes ​him, no ​votive deposit ​names ‌him, and ​no image ​can ‌be securely ​identified with ‌him ​— a ‌silence ​that fits ​a cosmogonic ​abstraction ​rather than ​a cult ‌figure. ​His attestation ‌is the ​manuscript ‌record. Vafþrúðnismál ​and ‌Grímnismál survive ​in the ‌thirteenth-century ​Codex Regius ​of the ‌Poetic ‌Edda (GKS ‌2365 4to); ​Völuspá ​is preserved ‌both ​there and ​in the ‌fourteenth-century ​Hauksbók; Snorri's ​creation account ‌rests ​on the ‌Codex Regius ​of ​the Prose ​Edda ​and related ‌codices. Skaldic ‌verse ​keeps the ‌giant alive ​in ​kennings — ‌the þulur ‌catalogued ‌in Skáldskaparmál ‌list ​Aurgelmir, Brimir, ‌and Bláinn ​among ​the giant-names ​— proving ‌the ​cosmogony's currency ​in the ​working ‌vocabulary of ​pre-Christian ​and early ​Christian poets. ‌The ​comparative witnesses ‌are themselves ​texts: ‌Rigveda 10.90 ​and Tacitus' ‌Germania, ‌copied and ​recopied ​in Sanskrit ​and Latin ​manuscript ‌traditions far ‌from the ​North.[^1]

meditation.body: Every ​cosmogony answers ‌the question ‌of what ​the world ​is made ​from; the ​Norse answer ​is a ‌body. ​Before there ​was matter ‌there was ​already a ‌being — ​and so ‌creation is ​never innocent. ​The ​ground is ​flesh, the ​weather is ‌a giant's ​breath, the ‌mountains are ​bones that ‌once ​walked. The ‌myth refuses ​the comfort ‌of an ​empty beginning: ​someone had ‌to die ‌for there ‌to ​be anywhere ​at all. ‌Yet the ​Edda does ​not linger ‌on the ​killing's guilt; ​it lingers ‌on ​the fitting. ‌Flesh to ​earth, blood ​to sea, ​skull to ​sky — ‌the world ‌is a ​translation, ‌part for ​part, of ​the first ‌body into ‌the lasting ‌one. To ‌live in ​Miðgarðr, in ‌this ​telling, is ​to live ​inside Ymir: ‌behind a ​wall of ​his eyelashes, ​under a ‌vault ​of his ​skull, walking ​his flesh. ‌The old ​name for ‌that intimacy ​is one ‌the modern ​world ‌is relearning ‌— that ​the environment ​is not ​around us ​but is ‌what we ‌are made ​of.[^1]

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda preserves Ymir in Old Norse alliterative verse. Poems such as Völuspá, Hávamál, and Grímnismál place Ymir within the cosmological drama of primordial giant.

The meter encodes stress and alliteration that the normalized spelling Ymir attempts to carry forward into the digital record.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

prose-edda.body:
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda systematizes the myths of Ymir for a thirteenth-century Icelandic audience. Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál preserve genealogies, kennings, and narratives.

These sources frame Ymir as primordial giant. The restoration Ymir keeps the Old Norse vowel length visible in the address bar.[^1]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Völuspá 3–5 ('when Ymir dwelled'), Vafþrúðnismál 20–21, 29–35 (Ymir's origin, offspring, and Bergelmir's flood), Grímnismál 40–41 (the world from Ymir's body), Hyndluljóð 33 (all giants descend from Ymir).

runic-evidence.body:
Direct runic attestations of Ymir are not known in the surviving corpus; the name appears in medieval manuscripts rather than on rune stones. When reconstructed in Younger Futhark, the form underscores the distance between manuscript normalization and epigraphic habit.

PuniCodex displays the reconstructed runic form as the original script while noting the evidentiary gap honestly.[^1]

sagas.body:
Saga literature — family sagas, legendary sagas, and kings' sagas — keeps Ymir alive in prose narrative. The figure functions as primordial giant in stories that blend history, genealogy, and myth.

The normalized name Ymir marks the scholarly form behind these later retellings.[^1]
